text.text: Adolescents with chronic academic stress may benefit from accessible, non-pharmacological approaches to stress management.

In this mixed-methods pilot study, six Grade 11 students completed a randomized, counterbalanced within-subject crossover design to compare the immediate effects of binaural-beat and singing-bowl listening.
Each condition was preceded by a 3-min baseline and followed by physiological, device-derived, subjective, and qualitative assessments.
Outcomes were heart rate, heart-rate variability (RMSSD), NeuroSky-derived Attention and Meditation indices, self-reported positive affect, negative affect, calmness, and open-ended reflections.
Physiological responses varied widely across participants and no clear condition-level advantage was observed for heart rate, RMSSD or affective ratings.
Five of six participants showed an increased NeuroSky-derived Meditation-index change in response to singing-bowl listening.
All six participants selected the singing-bowl condition as more effective in promoting relaxation.
In the qualitative reflections, people more often described the listening to singing bowls as calming, immersive and compatible with breathing.
The results are exploratory and do not demonstrate therapeutic superiority or neural entrainment.
They propose that perceptual comfort, attentional engagement and individual listening experience may be important components of sound-based stress regulation in adolescents.
Adolescence is a critical period for development when mental health problems can impact on well-being, learning and everyday functioning.
Mental disorders affect an estimated one in seven adolescents aged between 10 and 19, according to the World Health Organization [1].

text.text: Taken together, these results point to the need for accessible, low-risk approaches that may be beneficial for adolescents with regulation of short-term stress.
Non-pharmacologic approaches to stress reduction have included music and structured listening.
A large systematic review and meta-analysis reported beneficial effects of music interventions on physiological and psychological stress-related outcomes [7].

text.text: In this study, we examine two specific acoustic paradigms-singing-bowl listening and binaural-beat listening-which have been popularized in the relaxation literature but studied with different methodologies and populations.
The evidence for singing bowl interventions is still limited and focused on adult samples.
An observational study of 62 adults reported decreases in tension, anger, fatigue, and depressed mood following Tibetan singing-bowl sound meditation [9].

text.text: Collectively, these studies suggest possible relaxation-related effects, while also suggesting that the evidence base remains small and methodologically heterogeneous.

Binaural beats are an auditory illusion perceived when two tones of slightly different frequencies are presented separately to each ear, creating the perception of a beat at the frequency difference [13].

text.text: Existing research on singing bowls and binaural beats has therefore yielded mixed but potentially relevant findings, with much of the published evidence coming from adult or clinical settings rather than from adolescents [9] [10] [11] [12] [14] [15] [16] [17].

text.text: There seems to be especially little direct head-tohead evidence in high-school students comparing these two ways of listening.

The aim of this pilot study was to explore and compare short-term physiological, device-derived, subjective and experiential responses to binaural beats versus live singing-bowl sound in adolescents under examination period academic pressure.
This study therefore asks whether different sound-based listening modalities are associated with distinct patterns of relaxation.

Specifically, we examine whether relaxation is better understood as a frequency-specific neural response or as a broader psychophysiological experience emerging through interactions among sound, body, attention, and subjective perception.

Although binaural beats and singing bowls differ substantially in their acoustic and perceptual characteristics [9] [10] [11] [12] [13] [14] [15] [16] [17], the limited and heterogeneous existing evidence does not provide a sufficient basis for strong mechanism-specific predictions.

text.text: Accordingly, this pilot study adopted an exploratory approach.
We examined whether the two listening interventions were associated with different patterns of short-term change across physiological, device-derived, subjective, and experiential measures.
EEG-related observations were treated as exploratory and were not considered a definitive test of a brainwave-entrainment mechanism.

Hence the study examines whether the two listening conditions are associated with different patterns of short-term relaxation response rather than assuming a priori that they operated through different established mechanisms.
>Materials and Methods
text.formatted: <head n="2." >Materials and Methods</head>

text.text: Participants were recruited using convenience sampling from Beijing Haidian Future Academy (BHFA).
The sample consisted of six 11th-grade Chinese students (five female and one male), including five 17-year-olds and one 18-year-old.
Data collection took place during the school's final examination period.
All participants reported experiencing academic stress associated with preparation for their final examinations.

Because five of the six participants were minors, the study protocol was submitted to and approved by the Institutional Review Board (IRB) of Beijing Haidian Future Academy (BHFA), the research institution of the first author.
The study protocol was approved by the BHFA Institutional Review Board (Protocol No.
XXXX; approved Month Day, Year).
Ethical approval was obtained prior to the commencement of all participant-facing research activities and data collection.
Written informed consent was obtained from all participants and their parents or legal guardians prior to participation.
Participation was voluntary, and confidentiality procedures were implemented throughout data collection, analysis, and reporting.
All psychometric, physiological, and EEG-related data were de-identified and assigned numerical participant codes (e.g., Participant 1).
No personally identifiable information (PII) was included in the dataset used for analysis or manuscript preparation.
All participant-facing research activities and data collection were conducted by the first author at BHFA.

This study employed a randomized, counterbalanced within-subject crossover design to examine the immediate effects of two auditory interventions-singing bowl meditation and binaural beat meditation-on participants' physiological and subjective states.
Each participant completed both interventions, with intervention order determined using a random-number application.
Three participants completed the singing bowl intervention first, followed by the binaural beat intervention, whereas the remaining three completed the interventions in the reverse order.
Prior to the formal experiment, participants attended a pre-experimental instructional workshop designed to introduce the concepts and practices relevant to the study.
The workshop covered basic concepts related to brainwave activity, binaural beats, singing bowls, diaphragmatic breathing, and meditation posture.
Participants experienced and practiced singing bowl meditation during the workshop and were invited to verbally reflect on their experiences.
Because of time limitations during the workshop, binaural beat meditation was not conducted on site.
Instead, participants were provided with the binaural beat audio and instructed to complete at least one self-guided practice session at home before participating in the formal experiment.

Thus, all participants had prior exposure to both auditory interventions before formal data collection: singing bowl meditation through the in-person workshop and binaural beat meditation through subsequent at-home practice.
This familiarization procedure was intended to reduce stimulus novelty and ensure that participants understood the meditation procedures used in the experiment.
The formal experiment was conducted in the same enclosed classroom at Beijing Haidian Future Academy (BHFA) to minimize external auditory interference and environmental variability.
Room conditions, participant posture, breathing instructions, listening duration, and playback procedures were standardized across experimental sessions.
Participants and researchers remained in consistent locations within the room throughout data collection.
Each auditory intervention was preceded by a three-minute eyes-closed silent meditation baseline.
Following the first baseline, participants completed the first five-minute auditory intervention according to their randomized intervention order.
They subsequently completed a second three-minute eyes-closed silent meditation baseline before receiving the alternative fiveminute auditory intervention.

The second baseline provided a condition-specific resting measurement prior to the second intervention and allowed potential order and carryover effects from the preceding intervention to be considered in subsequent analysis and interpretation; it was not assumed to eliminate such effects.
The resulting experimental sequence was therefore: with the order of the singing bowl and binaural beat interventions counterbalanced across participants.
Two auditory conditions were used in the experiment: singing bowl sound and binaural beats.
Both conditions were designed as five-minute sound-based meditation experiences but differed substantially in their acoustic characteristics and mode of presentation.

For the singing bowl condition, a single singing bowl with a primary perceived pitch centered approximately on C4 was performed live by the experimenter in the same quiet classroom in which the formal experiment was conducted.
No additional music, drone, or recorded accompaniment was used.
Participants therefore listened to the natural attack, resonance, overtone structure, and decay produced by the bowl during live performance.
The same singing bowl and experimenter were used throughout the study to maintain consistency across participants.
For the binaural beat condition, a prerecorded stimulus was created using two closely spaced carrier frequencies selected in relation to the primary pitch of the singing bowl.

A 261-Hz carrier tone was presented to the left ear and a 267-Hz carrier tone to the right ear, producing a 6-Hz interaural frequency difference within the conventional theta-frequency range (4-8 Hz).
The stimulus was presented through in-ear headphones to enable independent delivery of the two carrier frequencies to the left and right ears, as required for binaural beat perception.

The use of 261 Hz as the reference carrier also provided an approximate pitch relationship between the binaural beat stimulus and the C-centered singing bowl condition, while preserving the distinct acoustic characteristics of the two interventions.
Upon arrival, participants were first asked to fill out a questionnaire with demographic and experiential information, such as previous music education and previous meditation experience.
Participants then completed a three-minutes eyes-closed silent meditation.
Physiological measures collected during this time served as the baseline for the first auditory condition.
Following the baseline period, participants were exposed to the first five-minute auditory intervention, either singing bowl sound or binaural beats according to the randomized condition order.
Physiological measures were obtained immediately following the intervention.
Participants then completed the same subjective ratings of positive affect (PA), negative affect (nA), and calmness and provided brief written reflections describing their listening experience.
Participants then participated in a second three-minute eye-closed silent meditation.

Physiological data collected during this period were used as the baseline for the second auditory condition and allowed potential carryover and order effects from the preceding condition to be considered in subsequent interpretation.
Participants then heard the alternative auditory intervention for five minutes.
The same physiological measurement and self-report procedures were repeated immediately following the intervention.
Participants again rated their positive affect (PA), negative affect (NA), and calmness and provided brief written reflections describing their listening experience.
At the end of the experiment, participants directly compared the two auditory interventions.

They indicated which intervention they perceived as more effective in promoting relaxation and provided a brief written explanation of their choice and the perceived differences between the two listening experiences.
Brain activity was monitored using a NeuroSky single-channel consumer EEG device.
The NeuroSky MindWave systems record from a frontal dry electrode and provides EEG-related frequency information together with proprietary device-derived indices [18].

text.text: In the present study, the visual display information related to alpha and theta together with the device derived Attention and Meditation indices were used.

We interpreted these outputs conservatively, since this consumer-grade single-channel EEG system is more susceptible to noise, artifacts, and measurement variability than research-grade multichannel systems [18, 19].

text.text: In addition， NeuroSky's Attention and Meditation eSense scores are proprietary indices ranging from 0 to 100 indices and should not be interpreted as direct clinical, psychometric, or conventional EEG measures [20].

text.text: Cardiovascular activity was monitored using an Apple Watch.
Heart rate (HR) and heart-rate variability (HRV) data were collected at the end of each measurement period, including the baseline and auditory-intervention periods.

HRV was summarized by the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD), a common time domain measure of HRV that reflects shortterm variation in heart rate and is frequently used as a surrogate measure of vagally mediated cardiac regulation [21, 22].
text.formatted: HRV was summarized by the root mean square of successive differences (RMSSD), a common time domain measure of HRV that reflects shortterm variation in heart rate and is frequently used as a surrogate measure of vagally mediated cardiac regulation <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">22]</ref>.

text.text: Unlike the continuously displayed EEG-related measures, HR and RMSSD values were recorded at discrete measurement points rather than continuously analyzed across each experimental period.

Because of the short measurement periods and the sensitivity of HRV to recording context, body position, respiration, and other methodological factors [21, 22], these values were considered exploratory physiological indicators rather than clinical measures.
text.formatted: Because of the short measurement periods and the sensitivity of HRV to recording context, body position, respiration, and other methodological factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">22]</ref>, these values were considered exploratory physiological indicators rather than clinical measures.

text.text: Subjective psychological states were measured using study specific 0-10 self-report ratings.
Three dimensions were measured: calmness, positive affect (PA), and negative affect (NA).
Participants provided these ratings immediately following each auditory intervention.

These brief ratings were designed to capture participants' immediate subjective responses for exploratory within-participant comparison and were not intended to function as validated diagnostic or psychometric scales.
In addition to the numerical ratings, participants provide brief written reflections after each auditory intervention.

At the end of the experiment, participants directly compared the two interventions by indicating which they perceived as more effective in promoting relaxation and providing a brief written explanation of their choice and perceived differences between the two listening experiences.

Together, the physiological, device-derived, and self-report measures provided complementary perspectives on participants' responses to the singing bowl and binaural beat interventions, allowing preliminary examination of both physiological patterns and subjective experiences of relaxation.

As this pilot study was exploratory in nature and the sample size was small (N = 6), statistical analyzes focused on descriptive statistics, within-participant change, individual response patterns, and convergence across multiple data sources rather than confirmatory hypothesis testing.
Analyzes were therefore primarily based on paired within-subject comparisons, as each participant was exposed to both the BB and SB conditions.
The sample size was very small and there was no defensible assumption of normality, so we used two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank tests to examine differences between conditions.
These analyzes were considered exploratory rather than confirmatory.
No correction for multiple comparisons was applied since the analyzes were exploratory and aimed at characterizing early response patterns rather than testing a family of confirmatory hypotheses.
Single p-values should therefore be interpreted with caution.
Importantly, statistical significance was not treated as equivalent to psychological or clinical importance.

The p-values were treated as measures of the compatibility of the observed data with a specified null model, rather than as direct measures of intervention efficacy or probability that a hypothesis was true [23].
text.formatted: The p-values were treated as measures of the compatibility of the observed data with a specified null model, rather than as direct measures of intervention efficacy or probability that a hypothesis was true <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">[23]</ref>.

text.text: Interpretation therefore focused on the direction and consistency of within-participant change, descriptive patterns of effect, convergence and divergence across physiological and subjective measures, and participants' reported listening experiences.
EEG alpha and theta activity were not analyzed as continuous quantitative outcomes .
Reliable mean alpha or theta power could not be calculated from the raw EEG time-series or calibrated spectral band-power data, so these were not retained in this study.
Instead, alpha-and thetarelated patterns were obtained from the single-channel NeuroSky visual display and qualitatively classified.
Thus, these observations were considered as descriptive supplemental data and not tested statistically by inferential means.
Participant open-ended reflections were retained verbatim and analyzed in conjunction with physiological and self-report outcomes to provide context for individual responses.

As formal independent coding and inter-rater reliability procedures have not yet been completed, these responses are currently treated as qualitative descriptive reflections rather than a formal thematic analysis.

text.text: Heart-rate responses varied substantially across participants and conditions.
Mean HR change was -5.00 BPM (SD = 12.60) following binaural beats and -2.67 BPM (SD = 7.00) following singing-bowl listening.
Median changes were -4.0 and -1.0 BPM, respectively.
The paired difference between conditions was not statistically distinguishable in this small sample, Wilcoxon W = 10.0, p= 1.00.
These findings indicate considerable individual variability and provide no evidence that either condition produced a consistently greater short-term HR reduction.
Participant-level changes further illustrate the substantial heterogeneity of heart-rate responses across both listening conditions (Figure 1).

text.text: HRV/RMSSD responses were also heterogeneous.
Mean change was +2.00 (SD = 4.20) following binaural beats and -2.17 (SD = 9.70) following singing-bowl listening.
The paired comparison was not statistically significant, W = 4.5, p = .563.
Thus, the current data do not support a condition-specific advantage in HRV response.
Given the small sample and short intervention periods, these measures are best interpreted as preliminary indicators of autonomic response variability.
Qualitative inspection of the NeuroSky display suggested participant-specific differences in alpha-and theta-related patterns across both listening conditions.
Observations related to alpha generally showed stable or increased display activity whereas observations related to theta were more variable across participants and conditions.
No consistent qualitative pattern was evident across the available recordings to support theta dominance.

These observations were not quantitatively analyzed, as the raw EEG time-series and calibrated spectral band-power data were not saved, and are not to be interpreted as evidence for or against cortical neural entrainment.
The NeuroSky-derived Attention index demonstrated substantial between-participant variability.
Mean change was 0.00 (SD = 29.66) following binaural beats and +7.50 (SD = 25.45) following singing-bowl listening.
The paired comparison was not statistically significant, W = 5.5, p = .375.

Because the Attention score is a proprietary device-derived index rather than a validated direct measure of attentional control, mindfulness, or cognitive load, higher or lower values were not interpreted as inherently more therapeutic.
A more consistent descriptive pattern was observed for the NeuroSky-derived Meditation index.
Mean change was -0.83 (SD = 24.58) following binaural beats compared with +15.00 (SD = 20.25) following singing-bowl listening.
Five participants demonstrated a more favorable Meditation-index change under the singingbowl condition, while one showed no between-condition difference.
The exploratory paired comparison did not meet the conventional .05 threshold, W = 0, p = .063.
Given the sample size, this result should not be interpreted as evidence of an established singing-bowl effect.

text.text: Under a simple two-choice null model, an exploratory exact binomial test yielded p = .031.
This result should nevertheless be interpreted cautiously.
Preference was an exploratory secondary outcome, the sample was extremely small, and participants could not be blinded to the perceptually obvious differences between the two auditory conditions.
Most importantly, preference should not be equated with intervention efficacy.
Qualitative reflections from participants help to contextualize this pattern of perceived comparative relaxation.
Singing-bowl listening was often characterized as calming, reduced mind-wandering, compatible with breathing, pleasurable, and immersive.

Binaural beats induced more heterogeneous responses, with some subjects reporting relaxation, and others describing the stimulation as mechanical, noisy, uncomfortable, cognitively distracting, or difficult to synchronize with their breathing rhythm.
At this stage these reflections are not offered as formally derived qualitative themes.
Instead, they offer a phenomenological background against which the large individual differences observed in the physiological and self-report measures can be understood.
>Discussion
text.formatted: <head n="4." >Discussion</head>

text.text: This mixed-methods pilot study explored the immediate psychological, physiological and experiential effects of listening to two different types of sound in adolescents.
The results do not suggest that listening to singing bowls is therapeutically superior to listening to binaural beats, nor do they suggest that either is clinically effective.

Due to the low number of participants, the high individual variability, the number of exploratory outcomes and the short duration of the intervention, such conclusions would be beyond the scope of the evidence of the study.

Instead, the findings offer initial evidence for a more complex applied psychological proposition; that sound-based stress regulation may be modulated, not just by the acoustic stimulus, but also by how the individual perceives, attends to and engages in the listening experience.
For at least some participants, both conditions were associated with relaxation.
However, physiological responses were heterogeneous and neither HR nor HRV showed a consistent advantage at the condition level.
Similarly, there were no statistically significant group differences in PA, NA, and Calmness at conventional levels.
The most consistent descriptive patterns were found for the NeuroSky-derived Meditation index, participants' qualitative experiences, and listening preference.
Five of the six participants showed a more favorable change in the Meditation index while listening to the singing bowl, and all six eventually preferred the singing-bowl condition.
The observations are hypothesisgenerating, not confirmatory.
An important consideration in interpreting these findings concerns the role of statistical significance.
With N = 6, the study has limited statistical power to detect anything other than very large and highly consistent effects.
Conversely, an isolated p value below .05 would not establish that an intervention is psychologically meaningful or clinically effective.
Accordingly, the present study does not treat the conventional p < .05 threshold as the primary criterion for interpreting the findings.
text.formatted: Accordingly, the present study does not treat the conventional p < .05 threshold as the primary criterion for interpreting the findings.

text.text: For example, the between-condition comparison for the NeuroSky-derived Meditation index yielded p = .063.
This should neither be dismissed as "no effect" nor reframed as statistically significant.
Instead, the directional consistency across participants constitutes a preliminary pattern worthy of replication.
Similarly, the unanimous preference for singing-bowl listening produced an exploratory binomial p = .031.
Although statistically notable under a simple choice model, this result concerns preference, not therapeutic efficacy.

Hence, the more informative question for an exploratory pilot study is not simply whether an outcome crossed a conventional significance threshold but whether multiple forms of evidence display coherent patterns that warrant further investigation.
The EEG-related observations require particularly cautious interpretation.
Binaural beats are often discussed when considering frequency-following or neural-entrainment hypotheses [13, 14, 17].
text.formatted: Binaural beats are often discussed when considering frequency-following or neural-entrainment hypotheses <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">[13,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">17]</ref>.

text.text: However, the present study was ill-equipped to provide a definitive test of cortical entrainment.
Raw EEG time-series and calibrated spectral band-power estimates were not saved.
Instead, alpha and theta patterns were observed by a single channel NeuroSky visualization and recorded descriptively.
Therefore, terms such as alpha increase, theta fluctuation or theta dominance refer only to the qualitative patterns observed in the visualization of the device.
They are not meant to be taken as quantitative evidence for changes in cortical oscillatory power.
Therefore, the present results neither show nor rule out neural entrainment.

There was no consistent qualitative pattern in the available NeuroSky visualization that was sustained and consistent with theta dominance, and the measurement protocol was insufficient to establish or rule out frequency-specific cortical entrainment.
This difference is important in that it suggests the theoretical assumptions of binaural beats are not being interpreted as empirical findings.
Similar caution is necessary when interpreting NeuroSky's proprietary Attention and Meditation indices [19,20] .

These device-derived scores are not equivalent to validated psychological measures of mindfulness, attentional regulation, meditation depth, cognitive load, or emotional relaxationand published evaluations of consumer-grade EEG devices also report substantial variability in such indices [19, 20].
text.formatted: These device-derived scores are not equivalent to validated psychological measures of mindfulness, attentional regulation, meditation depth, cognitive load, or emotional relaxationand published evaluations of consumer-grade EEG devices also report substantial variability in such indices <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">[19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">20]</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, an increased Meditation cannot be directly interpreted as evidence for "deeper meditation" just as a decreased Attention cannot be interpreted as beneficial cognitive disengagement.
These variables should therefore always be referred to throughout the manuscript as the NeuroSky-derived Attention index and NeuroSky-derived Meditation index.
In this pilot study, the main value of these measures is to provide an additional device-derived response measure that can be compared with physiological, self-report, and experiential data.
Some individual participants demonstrated substantial HR changes between baseline and postintervention measurements.
However, large pre-post differences should not automatically be attributed to the intervention.

Since participants performed two conditions within the same experimental session, baselines in the second condition could have been affected by the preceding intervention, the rest interval, adaptation to the experimental setting, expectancy about the second condition, or spontaneous physiological recovery.

For example, an intervention starting with an unusually high second baseline may seem to produce a particularly large HR reduction partly because of regression to the participant's usual resting state.

Therefore, the current design allows for describing observed within-condition physiological change, but not strong causal statements such as 'the intervention activated the parasympathetic nervous system'.
The interpretation of HRV is influenced by factors such as the recording time, respiration, posture, baseline conditions and other methodological factors [21, 22].
text.formatted: The interpretation of HRV is influenced by factors such as the recording time, respiration, posture, baseline conditions and other methodological factors <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">[21,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">22]</ref>.

text.text: Future studies should incorporate longer washout periods, testing on different days, or repeated baseline measurements.
One participant's response to singing-bowl listening is especially informative.
The participant stated that the sound was too loud and physically uncomfortable.
This was accompanied by a high negative effect and low calmness.
Rather than being treated solely as an outlier, this response may provide important information about individual differences in acoustic comfort and sensory tolerance.

Instead, it demonstrates a potentially important principle in applied psychology: Depending on the comfort of perception and the sensory tolerance of the individual, the same acoustic intervention may have a completely different psychological effect.
Sound intensity, timbre, temporal structure, as well as perceived naturalness and listener comfort [7, 8], may influence the way a sound intervention is experienced.
text.formatted: Sound intensity, timbre, temporal structure, as well as perceived naturalness and listener comfort <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>, may influence the way a sound intervention is experienced.

text.text: In the wider musicstress literature, context and reason for listening are also suggested to influence stress-related responses [7, 8].
text.formatted: In the wider musicstress literature, context and reason for listening are also suggested to influence stress-related responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: These features should thus not be understood solely as technical features but perhaps as elements of the psychological listening experience.

Future studies should include objectification of sound-pressure level calibration, documentation of listening level, safe and comfortable ranges, and consideration of allowing participants some limited control over playback intensity.
A clear and consistent finding in the present sample is the unanimous preference for singingbowl listening.

Nevertheless, preference can be the consequence of a variety of psychological processes such as pleasantness, familiarity, novelty, expectancy, perceived naturalness, cultural associations, esthetic preference or sensory comfort.
Preference cannot be equated with stress reduction, therefore."
At the same time, preference should not be necessarily treated as a nuisance variable.
It is plausible that sustained attention, expectancy and emotional responsiveness in applied listening interventions could be influenced by willingness to engage with the sound.
Research on everyday music listening suggests that stress-related effects may depend on the listening context and motivation [7, 8].
text.formatted: Research on everyday music listening suggests that stress-related effects may depend on the listening context and motivation <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">[7,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">8]</ref>.

text.text: Listener preference may be one of the factors in the process by which sound-based interventions affect subjective experience, but this study is unable to establish that mechanism.
This possibility deserves systematic investigation in larger studies.

The present findings, together with the inconsistent literature on binaural-beat entrainment [14, 17], suggest that a purely frequency-based account might not be enough to understand sound-based stress regulation.
text.formatted: The present findings, together with the inconsistent literature on binaural-beat entrainment <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">[14,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">17]</ref>, suggest that a purely frequency-based account might not be enough to understand sound-based stress regulation.

text.text: Instead of assuming a simple path like: acoustic frequency → pre-determined brainwave state → relaxation.
The present findings motivate investigation of a broader therapeutic listening framework.

In this preliminary framework, the psychological effects of sound-based listening may emerge through dynamic interactions among acoustic characteristics, perceptual comfort, attentional engagement, physiological regulation, affective response, and subjective meaning.

The present pilot data do not provide causal evidence for this sequence and, thus, Therapeutic Listening should be offered as a preliminary interpretive framework, and not as a validated theoretical model.
Nevertheless, the framework provides a useful applied psychological lens by shifting attention away from the question: What sound makes the desired brainwave?
to ask yourself: What are the acoustic, psychological and contextual conditions for a listening experience that facilitates stress regulation for a particular adolescent?
From the point of view of applied psychology this may be the more important question.

Results suggest that the value of sound-based interventions for adolescent stress regulation may not be in whether or not a particular stimulus induces a pre-determined neurophysiological state, but rather in how adolescents experience, engage with, and self-regulate via the listening experience.

Therapeutic Listening may thus provide a useful initial framework for exploring interactions among auditory features, perceptual comfort, attentional engagement, affective response, physiological regulation, individual preference, and subjective meaning-making.
Several limitations severely limit interpretation.
First, the sample size included only six adolescents.
So this study should be considered exploratory and hypothesis generating rather than an efficacy trial.
Secondly, the crossover design introduces potential order and carry-over effects.

Although we counterbalanced the order of conditions, the relatively short time between interventions may not have been sufficient for participants to return to their original physiological and psychological state.

Third, the use of a single-channel consumer-grade NeuroSky system, the lack of storage of raw EEG recordings, and reliance on proprietary indices and qualitative visualization limited the interpretation of EEG.
Comparative validation studies have shown that low-cost single-channel systems can capture usable EEG-related signals but are more noise-limited and less reliable than medical-grade systems [18, 19].
text.formatted: Comparative validation studies have shown that low-cost single-channel systems can capture usable EEG-related signals but are more noise-limited and less reliable than medical-grade systems <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">[18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">19]</ref>.

text.text: When neural entrainment is a primary research question, future research should use research-grade multichannel EEG with prespecified spectral analyzes.
Fourth, standardization and documentation of sound intensity should be more rigorous.
The negative effect in one participant shows that acoustic comfort can have a significant impact on psychological outcomes.
Fifth, the psychological outcome measures were brief and largely state-based.
Future studies with larger samples should include validated adolescent stress, anxiety, emotion-regulation, and mindfulness measures along with the physiological indices.
Sixth, blinding of the participants to the two acoustically different interventions was not performed, which could have led to expectancy and preference effects.

Seventh，although participants were familiarized with both interventions prior to formal data collection, familiarization occurred in different contexts: singing-bowl meditation was experienced in a supervised workshop, whereas binaural-beat familiarization was completed independently at home.
This difference may have introduced contextual or expectancy effects.

Finally, although open-ended responses provide valuable context about the experience, the present qualitative component should remain descriptive unless formal analytic procedures are conducted at a later time.
For future mixed-methods research, independent coding, either predefined or iterative codebook development, coder reconciliation, and proper assessment of coding reliability could be used.

This mixed-methods pilot study provides preliminary evidence that binaural beats and singingbowl listening may support short-term relaxation and stress regulation in adolescents, while also revealing substantial individual variability in physiological, device-derived, subjective, and experiential responses.
The findings did not establish frequency-specific neural entrainment, nor did they demonstrate the therapeutic superiority of either intervention.
However, singing-bowl listening showed a more favorable descriptive pattern in the NeuroSky-derived Meditation index and was preferred by all six participants.
Participants also more frequently described the singing bowl in terms of calmness, immersion, reduced mind wandering, and compatibility with breathing.
These findings should be interpreted cautiously given the small sample, potential order and carry-over effects, and limitations of the EEG measurement.
More broadly, the results suggest that sound-based stress regulation may not be adequately explained by acoustic frequency or presumed brainwave entrainment alone.

Instead, the psychological effects of listening may emerge through interactions among acoustic characteristics, perceptual comfort, attentional engagement, affective response, physiological regulation, individual preference, and subjective meaning.
We therefore propose Therapeutic Listening as a tentative applied psychological framework to study adolescents' interaction with sound-based interventions.

More controlled studies are needed using validated psychological measures, standardized acoustic parameters, and researchgrade physiological methods to see if these preliminary patterns replicate, and to clarify which listening experiences are most effective, acceptable and appropriate for adolescent stress regulation.
